title: Noisy-affinity autoscaler drift — incident capture and runbook draft
content:
Summary:

This doc is a first-pass capture of the Jan 17-18 2025 degradation event in the dedicated GPU pool (eu-west-1a). Symptoms: sustained increased tail latency for generation endpoints backed by the dedicated pool, elevated queueing and stall metrics, and several customer-reported timeouts. Root causes appear to be a combination of (A) tenant placement/affinity drift that concentrated several heavy multi-stream workloads on a subset of nodes (noisy neighbor), (B) autoscaler cooldown/min_replicas misconfiguration preventing timely scale-out, and (C) slow GPU memory reclamation / fragmentation that led to eviction pressure and degraded throughput.

Impact & scope:
- Affected capacity: dedicated-gpu-pool-eu-west-1a (8-node pool; 2 nodes effectively saturated)
- Customers impacted: 3 mid-market customers on Dedicated (support tickets opened), multiple hosted customers experienced fallback to lower-throughput paths when routing policies triggered
- Observable impact: per-request latency 95p increased from ~120ms to ~680ms for short-response models; token throughput dropped ~35% for the pool; autoscaler did *not* add nodes for ~22 minutes after initial queue growth

High-level timeline (UTC):
- 2025-01-17 21:03: first alert: qps queue depth crossed high-water mark (dcgm.work_queue_depth)
- 21:05: SRE paged; initial triage showed two nodes at >90% GPU util and high memory fragmentation reported by DCGM
- 21:10: increased host-level swap activity (rare), kubelet logs showing frequent pod evictions/restarts on Node-03
- 21:12: autoscaler event: scale-out requested but stayed pending due to min-ready-duration and cooldown settings (see details below)
- 21:27: autoscaler eventually provisioned 2 nodes; by then several requests had timed out and fallback routing triggered
- 21:45: temporary mitigation: moved noisy tenants via node-affinity override and adjusted scheduler tolerations to balance load
- 22:30: latency returned near-normal but residual throughput anomalies persisted until 02:00 due to GPU memory fragmentation requiring container restarts

Root cause analysis (hypothesis chain):
1) Placement/Affinity drift: a recent change in the placement controller (PR 482) unintentionally relaxed anti-affinity constraints for certain Dedicated tenants, allowing heavy batch/stream jobs to co-locate on the same nodes. The distribution change was subtle and only apparent under the week's new traffic pattern.
2) Noisy neighbor amplification: Those co-located workloads used many concurrent CUDA streams and pinned a lot of GPU memory. DCGM reported high "allocated_memory" and high "context_switch" counts. Multi-tenant MPS settings amplified interference, causing kernel stalls and higher scheduler latencies inside the runtime.
3) GPU memory fragmentation and slow reclamation: Model serving containers frequently loaded/unloaded large model shards. The NVIDIA driver + CUDA runtime observed fragmentation; the process of reclaiming memory (driver side) created spikes in latency and occasionally triggered host OOM-kicks for ephemeral helper processes, causing pod restarts.
4) Autoscaler config mismatch: autoscaler had cooldown=15m and min_replicas=2 for the pool. During the initial surge, the controller created scale requests but the nodes were not marked ready for >20m because of image-pull backlog in the zone and the min_ready_duration setting prevented faster scaling. The combination resulted in delayed scale-out exactly when it was most needed.

Detection notes:
- Primary signals: dcgm.gpu_utilization, dcgm.allocated_memory_bytes, node_pod_eviction_count, kubelet.eviction_time, autoscaler.pending_scale_requests, pod_restart_count
- Secondary: host swap usage (sar), dmesg OOM logs, nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.free,utilization.gpu,processes
- Gap: we had no alert correlating high fragmentation + high stream counts. Existing alerts are per-metric and did not escalate combined signal early enough.

Immediate mitigations executed:
- Identified noisy tenants and applied temporary node-affinity overrides to spread them across at least 4 nodes (manual sched-affinity in k8s) — reduced contention quickly
- Temporary lowering of autoscaler cooldown to 1m on the pool and set target_utilization thresholds more aggressive for 30 minutes (rollback scheduled)
- Restarted a small set of model-server pods on the two hot nodes to force driver memory reclamation (note: this caused short-lived 503s but reduced tail latency)
- Enabled emergency routing fallback to hosted fleet for the highest priority tenants to reduce customer-visible impact

Short-term action items (owners & ETA):
- A1: Revert the placement PR relaxation or add a safety gate for anti-affinity (owner: Arjun Patel, ETA: 2025-01-22)
- A2: Add combined-alert rule: (dcgm.memory_fragmentation > X) && (dcgm.concurrent_streams > Y) && (node.pod_evictions > 0) => P1 pager (owner: Marcus Lee, ETA: 2025-01-24)
- A3: Tweak autoscaler min_ready_duration and cooldown defaults for dedicated pools; add faster-path for "healthy but image-pull-slow" scenarios (owner: Sofia Alvarez, ETA: 2025-01-25)
- A4: Add a k8s scheduled job that runs a lightweight GPU defragmentation probe (nvidia-smi + small allocator test) to surface fragmentation earlier (owner: eng-serving-runtime, ETA: 2025-02-05)

Longer-term improvements / runbook additions:
- Runbook: "Noisy-Tenant Isolation for Dedicated Pools" (draft below)
- Scheduler changes: enforce stronger anti-affinity by default for dedicated-tenant pods with large-gpu-memory label; prefer spread plugin for pool nodes
- Autoscaler: add override where a detected queue-depth spike can trigger an "emergency scale" path that ignores image-pull backlog up to a limit (with opt-in/permission guard)
- Observability: new dashboards combining DCGM, kubelet eviction, and autoscaler pending queues for a single-pane-of-glass incident view
- Capacity policy: reserve 1 node headroom per pool for sudden noisy-tenant spikes (cost vs SLAs tradeoff)

Draft runbook: "Noisy-Tenant Isolation for Dedicated Pools"
- Symptoms: sudden increase in queue depth, two or more nodes with >85% GPU util + high allocated_memory and high pod_restart_count
- Preliminary checks (oncall):
  - kubectl get pods -n dedicated --field-selector status.phase=Running -o wide | grep <pool-name>
  - kubectl top pods --containers (look for pods with extreme GPU env vars)
  - dcgm-exporter query: 'dcgm.allocated_memory_bytes{pool="<pool>"}' and 'dcgm.concurrent_streams{pod=~".*"}'
  - nvidia-smi on suspect node: nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,process_name,gpu_memory_usage --format=csv
- Quick isolation steps:
  1) Identify top-3 memory-hog pods via dcgm and kubectl; cordon one hot node and evict lower-priority pods (kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force) OR apply nodeAffinity to move noisy pods elsewhere (kubectl patch deployment ...)
  2) If eviction rate is causing instability, perform controlled pod restarts for model-servers on hot nodes (kubectl rollout restart) to release driver-side fragmentation
  3) If autoscaler is not scaling: check autoscaler status (kubectl -n kube-system describe hpa/cluster-autoscaler or custom controller); if pending due to min_ready_duration, consider temporary override: 'kubectl edit cm autoscaler-config' set cooldown=60s and trigger a manual scale via API
  4) If image-pull backlog prevents node readiness, contact infra-region team to prioritize registry pulls or temporarily relax imagePullPolicy to use pre-warmed images (short-term)
- Communication: post incident summary to #oncall-prod with impacted tenant list and mitigation steps; open support tickets for affected customers

Open questions / follow-up research:
- Can we instrument and expose an explicit GPU fragmentation metric (driver-level) vs allocated vs used? Current DCGM metrics are noisy.
- Would switching heavy tenants to GPU MPS groups or dedicating entire GPUs (no MIG) for some classes reduce interference?
- What is the acceptable headroom policy for Dedicated pools given committed-reserved customers? (Finance/product tradeoff)
- Should we implement automated tenant throttling if per-tenant stream counts exceed threshold?

Appendix: useful commands / traces seen during incident
- dcgm-exporter query examples:
  curl -s 'http://dcgm-exporter.prod.svc:9100/metrics' | grep dcgm.allocated_memory_bytes | sort -nr | head -n 20
- nvidia-smi snapshot (example):
  nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,utilization.gpu,memory.total,memory.used --format=csv
- kubelet logs excerpt that correlated with pod restarts: 'eviction manager: nodefs.available is low, evicting pods' (we saw repeated entries on Node-03)

Notes to self (informal):
- This felt different from a pure autoscaler bug — the placement/affinity change created the surface for the noisy neighbor to bloom. Focus fix on placement safety-guard + better combined alerts.
- Keep the temporary autoscaler cooldown change in place for 48h while we monitor; schedule automatic rollback and post-change review.

Last action: opened follow-up tickets, assigned owners above, and scheduled 30-min postmortem sync on 2025-01-23 16:00 UTC to validate mitigations and finalize runbook.

Draft status: working notes, needs engineering + product input for headroom policy.

-- Priya Natarajan (oncall lead)
